title: Solomon's Divided Heart and the Kingdom Torn
summary: In old age Solomon's many foreign wives turn his heart to other gods, and he builds shrines for them outside Jerusalem. The LORD announces that he will tear most of the kingdom from Solomon's son, leaving one tribe for David's sake, and raises up adversaries: Hadad of Edom, Rezon of Damascus, and Jeroboam, to whom the prophet Ahijah gives ten pieces of a torn cloak. Solomon dies after forty years, and Rehoboam succeeds him.
story: The warning of 9:6-9 now begins to come true. The king who dedicated the temple builds high places for Chemosh and Molech within sight of it, and the golden age of chapters 3 to 10 ends in a single chapter. Everything that follows in 1 and 2 Kings grows out of this: the split into two kingdoms in chapter 12, the northern kingdom's long run of unstable dynasties, and Judah's survival as the house of David's one remaining tribe. The chapter also keeps God's promise to David alive. Judgment is delayed for David's sake, one tribe remains so that David will always have a lamp, and verse 39 ends Ahijah's oracle with a note of hope: David's descendants will be humbled, but not forever.
historical:
The adversaries of verses 14-40 show the edges of Solomon's power fraying. Hadad was an Edomite prince who escaped the slaughter recorded in 2 Samuel 8:13-14 and grew up at the Egyptian court; the Egyptian queen Tahpenes is not named in surviving Egyptian sources, and her pharaoh is not identified. Rezon seized Damascus, which from this point becomes the center of the Aramean kingdom that will trouble Israel for two centuries. Jeroboam, an Ephraimite official in charge of the labor gangs of the house of Joseph (the central tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh), fled to Shishak of Egypt. Shishak is Sheshonq I, founder of Egypt's Twenty-second Dynasty, who reigned roughly from 945 to 924 BC. He is the first pharaoh the Bible names, and his name is one of the fixed points for dating this period.

Chemosh, the god of Moab, is named in the Mesha Stele, a Moabite inscription from the ninth century BC in which King Mesha credits Chemosh with his victories over Israel. Milcom was the national god of Ammon. The hill east of Jerusalem is the Mount of Olives or a spur of it; 2 Kings 23:13 calls it the Mount of Corruption and records Josiah's destruction of these shrines about three centuries later. Verse 41 cites the Book of the Acts of Solomon, a lost royal source the writer of Kings used.
cultural:
Royal marriages in the ancient Near East were political. A foreign princess sealed a treaty, and she brought her household and her gods with her. Seven hundred wives of royal birth describe a vast network of alliances; three hundred concubines were secondary wives without the same status. Building shrines for a wife's national god was ordinary diplomatic courtesy in that world. For Israel it was precisely what the law forbade, since Deuteronomy 7:3-4 had warned that such marriages would turn Israel's heart to other gods. The concern in the text is religious, not ethnic: Ruth the Moabite, David's ancestor, joined herself to Israel's God.

Tearing a garment (verses 29-31) was a way of acting out a prophecy, a sign-act that made the word visible and, in the ancient understanding, set it in motion. It recalls the torn robe of Samuel in 1 Samuel 15:27-28, when the kingdom was torn from Saul. A lamp kept burning in a house was a picture of a family line continuing; to have one's lamp put out was to have one's household end.
literary: The chapter is built as an indictment followed by its consequences. Verses 1-8 describe the sin, with the word heart repeated (verses 2, 3, 4, 9) to show where the failure lies. Verses 9-13 give God's verdict in direct speech. Verses 14-40 then introduce three adversaries in turn, each with a short backstory, the third expanded into a prophetic scene. Key words link the parts. God will tear the kingdom (verses 11, 12, 13, 31), and Ahijah tears his new cloak. Solomon was not wholeheartedly devoted as David had been (verse 4), and Jeroboam is offered a lasting dynasty on the same terms (verse 38). The standard formula of verses 41-43 (sources, length of reign, death, burial, successor) is the pattern Kings will use for every king that follows.

outline.t: Solomon's foreign wives turn his heart to other gods
The LORD's verdict: the kingdom torn, one tribe kept for David
Ahijah's torn cloak and the promise to Jeroboam

doctrines.note: Solomon's idolatry did not begin with a decision to abandon the LORD; it grew from loves that pulled his heart in many directions. The chapter shows idolatry as a divided heart before it is a shrine on a hill.

God judges Solomon's unfaithfulness yet keeps his promise to David. One tribe remains, David keeps a lamp, and the humbling of David's line is not forever. God's covenant faithfulness outlasts the failures of the people he made it with.

The LORD raises up adversaries (verses 14 and 23) and gives the kingdom to whom he chooses. Human politics, exile, and ambition are real, and God is at work through them without being the author of the sins involved.

words.note: Satan, adversary. Here it is an ordinary noun for an opponent, used of Hadad and Rezon. Only in a few later texts (such as Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3) does it describe a heavenly accuser, and it becomes a proper name later still. Reading the devil into this chapter would be a mistake.

Shalem, whole or complete, from the same root as shalom. Solomon's heart was not whole with the LORD (verse 4). The contrast is with David, whose sins were great but whose loyalty to the LORD never went to other gods. Wholeness here means undivided allegiance.

Nir, lamp. God keeps one tribe so that David will always have a lamp before him in Jerusalem (verse 36). The image returns at key moments in Kings (15:4; 2 Kings 8:19) whenever the Davidic line survives a king who deserved to lose it.

Davaq, to cling or hold fast. Deuteronomy uses this verb for Israel's clinging to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20). Verse 2 turns it around: Solomon clung to these women in love. The word shows what took the place of God.

christ: The promise that David would always have a lamp, and that his line would be humbled but not forever, is one of the threads the Old Testament hands to the New. After the exile no son of David reigned, and the prophets spoke of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1), a king who would come from a line cut down. The Gospels open by presenting Jesus as that son of David (Matthew 1:1). Solomon's failure also sharpens the longing: the wisest king in Israel's history could not keep his own heart. The New Testament's answer is not a wiser Solomon but a king whose heart was wholly given to the Father, and who calls his people to love God with all their heart. This is a covenantal line of promise rather than a prediction within the chapter.

hard.q: How could the wisest man in Israel end like this, and are seven hundred wives meant literally?
hard.a:
The text does not treat wisdom as a guarantee of faithfulness. It says Solomon's heart turned when he grew old, gradually and through his loves. Many readers find this the chapter's sharpest lesson: understanding what is right and loving it wholeheartedly are different things. Proverbs, associated with Solomon, repeatedly warns about the very danger that undid him.

As for the numbers, some scholars think they are inflated royal language, as the figures for other ancient harems sometimes were; others take them as a real count of diplomatic marriages accumulated over forty years. Either way the narrator's point is the same: the king broke the law of Deuteronomy 17:17 on a scale that could not be missed, and the result was exactly the one that law predicted.

questions: Solomon's heart turned slowly, through things he loved. What loves in your life could, over years, divide your loyalty to God?
God judged Solomon but kept a lamp burning for David. Where have you seen God's faithfulness outlast human failure?
Jeroboam was offered the same terms as David. What does it suggest about God that he gives a new start with the same call to obedience?
